result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.k_shell()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Extract the k-shell subgraph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L43617-L43689){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.k_shell(k) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k-shell](/assets/graphs/k-shell.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the eight-node graph with a dense cluster A to D, a ring E, F, G and a pendant H. Right: the 2-shell holds the nodes whose coreness is exactly 2, so E, F, G and the edges E to F and F to G are in the accent color, while the 3-core A to D and the pendant H (coreness 1) are dashed." width="100%"} The k-shell contains nodes with coreness exactly equal to `k`. The coreness of a node is the highest `k` for which the node is part of the k-core. Equivalently, the k-shell is the k-core minus the `(k+1)`-core: the layer of nodes that is peeled away when going from one core to the next. The shells partition the graph, so every node belongs to exactly one of them. This "onion" view of a network is useful for: - locating nodes by how deep they sit, from the periphery (low `k`) to the core (high `k`) - studying a single layer, for example the nodes that are fairly well connected but not part of the innermost core - comparing how the layers are populated across networks The returned graph contains only the shell's nodes and the edges *between* them; edges that connect the shell to other shells are dropped, so the result can be sparse or even edgeless. To get every node's coreness at once, use `coreness()`; see also `k_core()` and `k_crust()`. Degrees count edges without weights. For directed graphs, degree means out-degree. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps the node and edge IDs, labels, weights and attributes of the original. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Coreness value to extract. Must be a non-negative integer. `k=0` gives the isolated nodes. If no node has coreness exactly `k`, the result is an empty graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the k-shell nodes and their connecting edges. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below has a dense cluster (A, B, C, D), a loop E-F-G attached to it, and a pendant node H. Its three shells split the nodes into the pendant (coreness 1), the loop (coreness 2), and the cluster (coreness 3): ::: {#d7a0a778 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "G"), ("G", "D"), ("G", "H")]) ) { k: sorted(graph.k_shell(k).get_node_df()["label"].to_list()) for k in [1, 2, 3] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {1: ['H'], 2: ['E', 'F', 'G'], 3: ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']} ``` ::: ::: Only edges inside the shell are kept. The 2-shell has the edges E-F and F-G, but the links from E and G into the cluster (and from G to H) are dropped: ::: {#b81f1bc2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} shell_2 = graph.k_shell(2) (shell_2.count_nodes(), shell_2.count_edges()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (3, 2) ``` ::: :::
